Players roll 4 standard dice and 1 shape die to determine the numbers they must fill in on their score sheet and the shape they must fill in. Players also have 5 block tiles they can use to block another's stack. As in Tetris, the game ends when a stack reaches the top. The player with the highest score wins. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary For tips on how to play number drop, see Tips_numberdrop Contents 1 Goal 2 Summary 3 Game Play 3.1 Phase 1: Roll the dice 3.2 Phase 2: Block others 3.3 Phase 3: Drop a shape 3.4 Phase 4: Create a combo 3.4.1 Block activation 3.5 Phase 5: End the turn 4 End of the game Goal The goal of Number Drop is to have the most points at the end of game. To do this, players compete by dropping placing numbers and dropping shapes to earn identical or sequenced number combinations. Summary Place numbers and drop shapes to create combinations of identical or consecutive numbers on their grid. Be the most efficient and drop penalties onto your opponents! As soon as a player reaches the Game Over line, the game ends and whoever has the most points is the winner. Will you reach the ultimate score of 100? Game Play Each turn, both players receive the same number and shape options. Players decide how to use these options and place them on their board. At the end of the turn, these choices are revealed for other players to see. There are 4 phases to each turn, with a possible 5th if blocking has been activated: Roll the Dice Block (if applicable) Drop a Shape Create (claim) a Combo End Turn (score) Phase 1: Roll the dice The BGA adaptation of Number Drop will handle this phase for you. 5 dice (4 number dice and 1 shape die) are rolled each turn. The shape die has 4 shape options and a star which represents a wild card (you choose your shape). The number dice contain numbers 1 - 7, as well as stars (wild). The stars may be used as any number from 1 - 7, as well as 0, 8, or 9. If blocking was activated in the previous turn AND any of the die reveal a star, phase 2 begins. Otherwise, players proceed to phase 3. Phase 2: Block others A block is a penalty shape that will hinder the opponents. Its activation is described in phase 4 . Phase 2 occurs only if: There are active blocks c ircled but not crossed off AND There is at least one star on the dice roll (on any die). Otherwise, go to phase 3 . Check all the circled blocks of all the players. If there are several circled blocks , only take into account the one (not crossed off) on the higher line. A, then B, then C... The other active blocks will be taken into account the next time there is a star in the dice results. All the players that have not circled that block must then drop the corresponding shape on the board into their grid. The shape is composed of X's. It can be rotated or flipped freely, and it follows the shape placement rules . Once the shape is placed, it is circled. It cannot be used for combinations but can complete lines . Then, all players cross off the penalty block on their score sheets and the tile is removed from the board. It cannot be used again. Players can still create the matching combinations for scoring purposes. The turn is over. The player to the left of the first player becomes the new first player and starts a new turn on phase 1 . Phase 3: Drop a shape Each player, simultaneously, chooses the way they want to combine the dice (in their head) before writing down the result on their sheet: They must use the 4 numerical dice for their value. They must use those values by placing them in the shape indicated by the shape die, in any orientation. The shape can be turned and flipped: The stars are wilds: on a numerical die, each player can pick any number between 0 and 9. On the shape die, each player can choose the shape they want among the shapes present on the die. Phase 4: Create a combo Every player can create only one combination each turn, star

[Rating: 3/10] Played on BGA. Didn't like it as much as I thought I would, somehow felt restrictive and annoying at times.

[Rating: 3.5/10] This would have worked much better without the attack blocks, I think, but I also don't think it's worth house-ruling that into the game.

[Rating: 3.5/10] I don't like playing board games alone. In this game it doesn't matter if you play with others. The theme is quite nice though.

[Rating: 4/10] It tried, it really did.  But ultimately this is a R&W that works but I have 0 interest to see again.

[Rating: 4/10] Pleasant enough but too random for me with no forward planning. The scoring is tight, but it's also extremely difficult to pull off making the whole game a bit frustrating.

[Rating: 4/10] Me da los mismos vibes que el Roll to the Top y prefiero este ultimo. Concepto interesante, pero esto en app sería mucho mejor.

[Rating: 4/10] Solitaire Tetris simulation. I might continue with it at some point, but it lacks the appealing simplicity of NMBR 9 or the best roll-and-writes.

[Rating: 5/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  Another roll and write but one where you try to create sets or runs of numbers that are placed based on various tetris shapes. At different times, an odd shape will crash down and force you to react and work around. I'm uncertain how I feel about the game end condition - ends as soon as someone places a piece so it goes over the red line - which means you do have to pay attention to what others are doing since if they are ahead they could theoretically end the game by placing a piece accordingly once it gets to a certain point.

[Rating: 5/10] Tetris + roll-n-write. Not a whole lot else to say, except the scoring mechanism feels off in some way to me. Similar to Trek 12, but I'd probably rather play Trek 12 if I had to choose.

[Rating: 5/10] Each turn one common die determines what 4-space tetromino you can place in your roll-and-write pad (dropping it virtually from the top Tetris style) and the other 4 common dice determine what numbers you place into each space of the tetromino. You're aiming to get numbers in sequences and sets of different lengths, but each can only be scored once. It doesn't sound bad in theory and I didn't mind the puzzle but in practice too many players were paralysed on too many turns with the wealth of options on how to orient and place the shape and the numbers within to link up with already placed numb

[Rating: 5/10] Played on BGA - would rather play Tetris, and have ability to do "last minute scoot" to get a brick under another one.  Reprint KS Aug 2025 - https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/alderac/into-the-fun-factory-from-aeg/rewards  #LetterN #BGA

[Rating: 5/10] Learned on BGA. Simple roll n write game with a Tetris theme. Really doesn't offer much that is new, I think I would just rather play Brikks.

[Rating: 5/10] A delightful idea. The scoring mechanisms mean a lot of dead areas; people who deep in their bones expect a winning roll'n'write scoresheet to be nearly perfect (which apparently I do) may find this persistently unsatisfying. Also, the pain of losing the race to drop a punishment piece is... well, despite this having some elements I love that I haven't seen anywhere else, it's still a 5 for me. Playable, fun, but other things are more fun.

[Rating: 5/10] Roll and Write that tries to replicate the popular Tetris game. Lacks the speed rush of the original.

[Rating: 5/10] It is not even in the top 10 roll and writes I've played. It is a fine game, like, just very middle of the road in terms of the puzzle and stuff of it, but it just isn't interesting enough to set itself apart in the end.
